\section[il casello]{il casello — the toll booth (on the motorway)}

\label{lesson:IT-C405-casello}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for exactly, then the Italian for almost.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: il casello}
\textbf{il casello} — \textquotedblleft{}the toll booth (on the motorway)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Al casello paghiamo con la carta.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{At the toll booth we pay by card.}
\end{quote}

On the motorway you take a ticket at the first \emph{casello} and pay at the last one.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{casello} is built on \emph{casa} 'house' with the small-size ending \emph{-ello}: first the keeper's little house beside a road or a railway line. \emph{Casa} is inherited from Latin \emph{casa} 'cottage, hut' (EtymDB).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il casello}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{il casello}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{il casello}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for exactly, then the Italian for almost, then say \emph{il casello} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does il casello mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The toll booth (on the motorway)\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[la corsia]{la corsia — the lane (of a road); the ward (in a hospital)}

\label{lesson:IT-C405-corsia}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for almost, then the Italian for the toll booth.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la corsia}
\textbf{la corsia} — \textquotedblleft{}the lane (of a road); the ward (in a hospital)\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Resta nella corsia di destra.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Stay in the right-hand lane.}
\end{quote}

\emph{La corsia di emergenza} is the hard shoulder; in a hospital, \emph{la corsia} is a ward.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{corsia} is built on \emph{corsa} 'run, course', which goes back to Latin \emph{currere} 'to run' (Lewis \& Short): a lane is a strip to run along. The words are inherited from Latin.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la corsia}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la corsia}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la corsia}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for almost, then the Italian for the toll booth, then say \emph{la corsia} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la corsia mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The lane (of a road); the ward (in a hospital)\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[la tangenziale]{la tangenziale — the ring road, the bypass}

\label{lesson:IT-C405-tangenziale}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the toll booth, then the Italian for the lane.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la tangenziale}
\textbf{la tangenziale} — \textquotedblleft{}the ring road, the bypass\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Prendiamo la tangenziale per evitare il centro.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Let us take the ring road to avoid the centre.}
\end{quote}

It runs round the edge of a city and touches it like a tangent.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{tangenziale} is built on \emph{tangente} 'tangent', a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{tangēns} 'touching', from \emph{tangere} 'to touch' (Lewis \& Short): the road touches the city without crossing it.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for the toll booth, then the Italian for the lane, then say \emph{la tangenziale} again

\section[lo svincolo]{lo svincolo — the junction, the slip road}

\label{lesson:IT-C405-svincolo}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the lane, then the Italian for the ring road.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: lo svincolo}
\textbf{lo svincolo} — \textquotedblleft{}the junction, the slip road\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Esci al prossimo svincolo.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Get off at the next junction.}
\end{quote}

Where you leave the motorway or move from one big road to another.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{svincolo} is built on \emph{svincolare} 'to set free from a bond', from \emph{s-} and \emph{vincolo} 'bond', a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{vinculum} 'bond, link' (EtymDB): the road that lets you loose.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for the lane, then the Italian for the ring road, then say \emph{lo svincolo} again

\section[sorpassare]{sorpassare — to overtake}

\label{lesson:IT-C405-sorpassare}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Italian for the ring road, then the Italian for the junction.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sorpassare}
\textbf{sorpassare} — \textquotedblleft{}to overtake\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Il camion ci ha sorpassato a destra.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The lorry overtook us on the right.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Il sorpasso} is the act of overtaking; \emph{vietato sorpassare} — no overtaking.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sorpassare} is built from \emph{sor-}, a worn form of Latin \emph{super} 'over', and \emph{passare} 'to pass', which is inherited from Vulgar Latin \emph{passāre}, built on Latin \emph{passus} 'a step' (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\raggedright

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{sorpassare}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{sorpassare}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Italian for the ring road, then the Italian for the junction, then say \emph{sorpassare} again
\end{itemize}
